content: 1. The implementation of EPS (Essential Palliative Services) ensures that priority services for the majority of patients are established within a relatively short timeframe. This involves a tiered training approach for healthcare providers at various levels of care. 2. Basic training, lasting 20–40 hours, is provided to healthcare providers working at the primary and community levels to equip them with foundational palliative care skills. 3. Intermediate-level training, spanning 60–80 hours, is offered to physicians and nurses managing cancer patients at secondary and tertiary care levels. This training focuses on enhancing their ability to address the complex needs of these patients. 4. Proficiency or specialized training, lasting 3–6 months, is delivered to specialized teams or palliative care units operating at secondary and tertiary levels. This advanced training ensures expertise in managing complex palliative care cases. 5. Undergraduate training in palliative care is integrated into medical and nursing school curricula. The African Palliative Care Association has developed a core palliative care curriculum and a framework of core competencies, which have been adopted by some African countries. 6. The European Association for Palliative Care (EAPC) has also developed a set of core competencies for palliative care professionals, which serve as a guideline for training and practice. 7. Numerous free online training courses and resources are available to strengthen palliative care education and delivery at primary care and undergraduate levels. 8. A collaborative project called Transforming the System was initiated in Latin America by representatives from the International Association for Hospice and Palliative Care (IAHPC), Fundación FEMEBA (Argentina), and the Department of Palliative Medicine at Aachen University (Germany). The project aimed to promote the teaching of palliative care in medical and nursing schools and integrate it into undergraduate curricula across the region. 9. The project was piloted in Colombia between 2014 and 2015. It involved several steps, including initial visits to six universities to assess perceptions and interest in palliative care, a workshop to identify undergraduate-level palliative care competencies, and the development of educational materials in both Spanish and English. 10. Participants in the workshop, which included representatives from 17 medical and nursing schools in Colombia, reached a consensus on the competencies required for undergraduate palliative care education. These competencies were distributed and made available online for educational purposes. 11. Universities are now using these competencies as a model to develop their own palliative care curricula, tailored to the needs of their patients and the educational requirements of their students. 12. A third stage of the project, planned for December 2015, aimed to demonstrate innovative methods of teaching palliative care using the materials developed during the workshop. Similar approaches were planned for other Latin American countries, including Argentina in 2016. 13. Public education and awareness are critical to ensuring that individuals who need palliative care can access the necessary services. The general public must understand what palliative care entails, who should be referred for these services, and how patients and families can benefit from palliative care programs. 14. Policymakers must recognize that palliative care is an integral part of the continuum of care for diseases such as cancer and HIV/AIDS. It can be integrated into existing healthcare systems at relatively low cost and requires the availability of opioids across all levels of care. 15. The media plays a vital role in disseminating reliable information about palliative care. Journalists can help raise awareness by sharing stories of patients with advanced illnesses who emphasize the importance of pain relief for their quality of life. Safeguards should be in place to ensure that the dignity and rights of patients and their families are respected. 16. National palliative care standards are essential for establishing and operating palliative care services. These standards outline the necessary components of care, including governance, eligibility criteria, interdisciplinary team composition, required qualifications and training, and recommended staffing ratios. 17. Indicators to measure the structure, process, and outcomes of palliative care are crucial for evaluating and improving service quality. These indicators help authorities determine the value of palliative care within the national healthcare system and ensure access to quality services. 18. Continuous quality improvement is a fundamental commitment for all palliative care providers. Data collected from quality indicators serve as a primary source of information for enhancing services. 19. Measuring the quality of palliative care involves standardized clinical tools to assess symptom burden and functional ability. Challenges in measurement include the difficulty of communication with very ill patients and the limitations of family members in evaluating the patient’s experience. 20. The African Palliative Care Association has developed standards for providing quality palliative care across Africa. These standards address the unique challenges of home-based care, which relies heavily on volunteers, and emphasize the importance of maintaining acceptable standards of patient care. 21. The Hospice Palliative Care Association of South Africa (HPCA) has implemented an accreditation system with a star-rating framework to assess the development of palliative care services. This system includes an online self-assessment tool and external accreditation visits to ensure quality assurance. 22. Evidence indicates that palliative care, whether delivered through hospice, hospital-based, or home-based care, results in reduced healthcare costs and more appropriate use of healthcare resources. Measuring the utilization of healthcare resources, particularly inpatient care, is essential for evaluating the cost impact of palliative care. 23. Public attitudes toward palliative care and the relief of suffering can be measured through standardized surveys. These surveys assess the public’s understanding of palliative care and their perceptions of its importance in the context of life-threatening illnesses. 24. The European Association for Palliative Care has developed consensus-based norms and standards for hospice and palliative care in Europe. These standards serve as models for countries to develop their own national standards. 25. National standards for palliative care should include governance, eligibility criteria, interdisciplinary team requirements, training and education, clinical assessment, record-keeping, safety policies, and continuity of care. They should also address ethical issues, quality assessment, and the provision of care in various settings and for special populations. 26. The African Palliative Care Association’s standards for quality care target all providers and trainers involved in caring for individuals with life-threatening illnesses. These standards define the quality requirements for each level of service delivery, from primary/basic to tertiary/specialist care. 27. The HPCA accreditation system in South Africa provides a framework for monitoring community-based organizations and promoting quality palliative care for patients and families.
